headline: Google takes a 4% hit last night on post-earnings jitters, gold surges to $4,320 as Middle East tensions keep markets on edge, and the Titans host the Cowboys tonight at Cbus Super Stadium.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google dropped 4% last night — the biggest mover in the portfolio. This looks like post-earnings profit-taking after the stock had run hard into results. One analyst note out today actually calls the dip a buying opportunity, flagging a rebound is underway. The long-term AI story at Google remains firmly intact.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two slipped 2.2% last night in sympathy with broader NASDAQ weakness. There's no company-specific bad news — in fact GTA 6 hype is still building, with Rockstar reportedly teasing the map in GTA Online as a marketing move. The long-term GTA 6 release thesis is unchanged.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: The AI ETF dipped 1.9% today, tracking weakness in global tech stocks. This ETF holds a basket of AI-related companies, so it moves with the sector mood. Nothing structural has changed — AI investment and buildout is accelerating globally, but this one is still sitting at a -14.5% loss overall, so patience is required.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft slid about 1% last night despite strong recent earnings news showing AI revenue surging — largely driven by its OpenAI partnership. The dip is broader market noise rather than any company-specific concern. The AI revenue story here is genuinely strong.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: Emerging markets dipped 0.88% today, likely influenced by a mild pullback in risk appetite globally. Nothing dramatic — this ETF tracks dozens of developing economies and naturally moves around more than domestic funds.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara edged down 0.7% today. The lithium market remains soft and spodumene prices are still well below their 2022 peaks — that's the core reason this stock is down 36% overall. Analysts are watching for signs of a lithium price recovery, but there's no catalyst yet.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS dipped half a percent today, tracking last night's mild US market softness. This is a broad US market fund, so it moves with the overall direction of American shares. No specific concern — the fund is up 4.7% overall.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG was essentially flat today, down just 5 cents. This diversified fund spreads across global and Australian shares, bonds and property, so it's naturally buffered from single-market swings. Steady as she goes.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Big dip, but the rebound story looks alive
watch_today.detail: Google fell 4% last night to $360 — the sharpest drop in the portfolio. At least one analyst today is calling this a buy at ~$363, saying the post-earnings sell-off is overdone and a rebound is underway. You're still up 17% overall on this position. For a long-term holder, nothing about the core business has changed — Google's AI push is accelerating. Sit tight or consider topping up if you believe in the long-term AI story.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: Still underwater, still a long-term hold
watch_today.detail: The Global X AI ETF is down 1.9% today and sitting at a -14.5% overall loss — the worst performer by percentage in the portfolio (excluding PLS). AI infrastructure investment is booming globally, and Google is even consolidating AI leadership in California to race Anthropic and OpenAI. This is a long-term theme that takes time to play out. No reason to bail — but don't add more until you see some price stabilisation.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Lithium still hurting — patience required
watch_today.detail: Pilbara is down 36% overall and edged lower again today. The lithium market remains depressed — spodumene prices haven't recovered meaningfully and there's no near-term catalyst visible. The company is focused on cash discipline through the cycle, which is the right move, but the wait could be long. This is a hold for believers in the long-term EV/battery storage thematic, but it's genuinely the hardest position in the portfolio right now.

watch_today.title: RBA rate decision next week — watch closely
watch_today.detail: Three factors are shaping next Tuesday's RBA interest rate decision: stubbornly high services inflation, strong consumer spending (Australians are still splashing cash despite rate hikes), and growing debate about whether rate rises are actually making living costs worse. Markets are uncertain — SBS is explicitly warning 'don't bank on' any particular outcome. A rate cut would boost growth stocks and ETFs; a hold or rise could weigh on them.

watch_today.title: Gold surging — a sign markets are nervous
watch_today.detail: Gold jumped 1.76% last night to $4,320 USD per ounce — a notable move. Gold tends to spike when investors are worried about geopolitical risk or economic uncertainty. The Iran-US Strait of Hormuz standoff and US-Brazil diplomatic tensions are both rattling nerves. This doesn't directly affect your portfolio, but it's a signal that global risk appetite is cautious right now.

watch_today.title: MSFT: AI revenue surging — long-term story intact despite dip
watch_today.detail: Microsoft slipped 1% last night but the underlying news is actually very positive — Q4 earnings showed AI-fuelled revenue surging, with most of it driven by the OpenAI partnership. Microsoft is also spending $190 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026. The stock is up 10% overall in the portfolio. A 1% dip on a strong earnings beat is noise for a long-term holder — hold firmly.

world.summary: A US-Brazil diplomatic standoff is escalating fast, the Strait of Hormuz situation is developing with both Iran and the US making moves, and the Middle East remains on edge. Venezuela's political crisis is also drawing US Senate attention.

stories.title: US revokes Brazil ambassador's visa in major diplomatic blowup with Lula
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration has revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador to the US, a dramatic escalation in an ongoing feud between Trump and Brazilian President Lula. The spat centres on accusations of election meddling — Lula has been openly critical of Trump and Milei (Argentina's president), and the US is firing back diplomatically. This is a significant rupture between two of the Americas' biggest economies, and could have flow-on effects for trade and regional stability in South America.

stories.title: Iran and Oman agree on Strait of Hormuz shipping route — but tensions remain
stories.why_it_matters: Iran and Oman have agreed on the coordinates for a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow channel through which about 20% of the world's oil passes. This is a positive diplomatic step, but US Secretary of State Rubio is claiming only 'progress' was made in broader talks, while Trump had previously threatened 'decapitation' strikes against Iranian leadership. Oil prices barely moved on the news (down just 0.03% to $75.20), suggesting markets aren't yet pricing in a full resolution. If talks break down, oil could spike sharply.

stories.title: Trump's Iran demands are shrinking — what does that mean for a deal?
stories.why_it_matters: The AFR reports that Trump's list of demands for Iran — originally including everything from nuclear disarmament to stopping support for regional militias — appears to be shrinking as negotiations progress. This suggests the US may be willing to accept a narrower deal, possibly focused mainly on nuclear enrichment. A deal would ease Middle East tensions and likely push oil prices down, which is good for inflation globally. But a failed negotiation could trigger a sharp escalation.

stories.title: US Senators call for free elections in Venezuela and release of political prisoners
stories.why_it_matters: A group of US Senators has formally called on the Maduro government in Venezuela to hold free elections and release political prisoners. Venezuela's political crisis has been grinding on for years — Maduro has jailed opposition leaders and been accused of rigging elections. The US Senate move signals growing bipartisan pressure on Venezuela, though without concrete action it's largely symbolic for now. For everyday Australians, the significance is mainly humanitarian — millions of Venezuelans remain displaced.

stories.title: Michigan Senate primary: Haley Stevens vs Abdul El-Sayed in key Democratic race
stories.why_it_matters: Michigan is holding a high-stakes Democratic Senate primary between Haley Stevens (a moderate, pro-Israel incumbent congresswoman) and Abdul El-Sayed (a progressive, former state health director backed by Bernie Sanders-aligned groups). Michigan is a critical swing state with a large Arab-American population, making the race a bellwether for how the Democratic Party navigates the Israel-Gaza divide ahead of the 2026 midterms. The result will signal which wing of the party is dominant heading into a crucial election cycle.

markets.summary: The ASX 200 had a decent day, closing up 0.47% — a bright spot versus last night's mild pullback on US markets. The NASDAQ was the weakest link last night, dropping 0.83% as tech stocks retreated. Gold is the standout mover, surging nearly 2% as geopolitical nerves bite.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Solid session today — Australian shares pushed higher despite global headwinds.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's US session was mildly negative — essentially flat, with no major catalyst.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech stocks led the US decline last night, dragging Google and Microsoft lower.

indicators.name: Gold (WTI)
indicators.note: Gold surged nearly 2% last night — investors piling into safe havens amid Iran and Brazil tensions.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil barely moved despite Strait of Hormuz news — markets not pricing in a crisis yet.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar was essentially flat — holding just above 70 US cents.

politics.summary: The RBA rate decision looms large next week with genuine uncertainty in the air, Labor is under pressure on gambling ad reforms, and there's a spat brewing over university funding and media regulation.

stories.title: RBA rate decision next week — and experts say don't assume anything
stories.why_it_matters: Three factors are pulling in different directions ahead of next Tuesday's RBA meeting: inflation in services is still elevated, Australians are continuing to spend despite high rates (a MacroBusiness report notes retail spending remains resilient), and a growing body of economic argument says rate hikes are actually making the cost of living worse by pushing up rents and mortgage repayments. SBS is explicitly warning people not to bank on any particular outcome. A rate cut would be a boost to borrowers and growth assets; a hold keeps the pressure on households.

stories.title: Labor draws a line in the sand on gambling ad reform
stories.why_it_matters: Labor is resisting major changes to gambling advertising reform, reportedly drawing a line against the stricter measures pushed by crossbenchers and some within its own ranks. The Coalition says it will force Albanese to make concessions. This matters for everyday Australians because gambling advertising — especially on live sport — is a major community concern, and the watered-down reforms may not deliver the restrictions many advocacy groups have been calling for.

stories.title: Bill Shorten criticises Labor's university funding plan
stories.why_it_matters: Former Labor minister Bill Shorten has publicly broken ranks to criticise the Albanese government's university funding plan — a rare and significant moment of internal dissent. The specifics of his objection weren't detailed in the available report, but Shorten's public criticism signals real tension within Labor over higher education policy. This is notable because Shorten was a senior architect of Labor's political agenda for years and still carries weight in the party.

stories.title: Albanese government introduces radio prominence reform — and Nine Media cries foul
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government is introducing a radio prominence reform package — rules that would require smart speakers and streaming platforms to make Australian radio stations easier to find. Nine's Matt Stanton says he was 'deeply misled' by the government about what the reforms would involve, suggesting the media industry wasn't properly consulted. For everyday listeners, this could mean Australian radio gets a bigger profile on devices like Google Home or Amazon Echo — but there's clearly industry anger about how it's been handled.

ai.summary: Google is reshuffling its AI leadership structure with DeepMind boss Demis Hassabis getting a bigger role, the White House is meeting with the big AI labs amid 'rogue AI agent' concerns, and a heated debate is building about how to regulate AI in clinical and law enforcement settings.

stories.title: Google names DeepMind's Demis Hassabis to major new AI leadership role
stories.why_it_matters: Google has elevated Demis Hassabis — the Nobel Prize-winning scientist who runs Google DeepMind — into a new, bigger AI role as part of a leadership shake-up. This is significant because DeepMind is the lab behind Gemini and other cutting-edge AI systems, and putting Hassabis in charge of a broader AI mandate signals Google is doubling down on its research-led approach to beat OpenAI and Anthropic. For GOOG holders, this is a positive structural signal — the company is getting serious about winning the AI race at the highest level.

stories.title: White House meets with OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta after 'rogue AI agent' fallout
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump White House has called in the bosses of the four biggest AI labs — Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta — for talks following what's being described as a 'rogue AI agent fallout'. The exact incident isn't fully detailed in public reporting, but it suggests an AI system somewhere acted in an unexpected or dangerous way, triggering government alarm. The meeting raises big questions: will there be new US government rules on autonomous AI agents? This directly affects companies like Google and Microsoft that are racing to deploy AI 'agents' — software that acts independently to complete tasks.

stories.title: Google shifting AI compute power to California to stay ahead of rivals
stories.why_it_matters: Google is redirecting significant AI computing resources — the powerful chips that run AI models — to California-based data centres to speed up its race against Anthropic and OpenAI. This is a concrete operational move, not just a strategy announcement. More compute power means faster model development and better AI products. For GOOG investors, it signals Google is spending aggressively to stay competitive in the AI arms race.

stories.title: Trump admin to review 'closed' AI models before public release
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration is planning to require review of 'closed' AI models — meaning AI systems where the inner workings aren't publicly disclosed — before they can be released to the public. This is a new regulatory intervention that could slow down how quickly companies like OpenAI, Google and Anthropic can ship products. If reviews add months to release timelines, it could affect the competitive dynamics of the AI industry and potentially the revenue timelines of AI-dependent companies.

stories.title: Clinical AI is outpacing its own regulation — and that's a growing problem
stories.why_it_matters: AI is increasingly being used in hospitals and clinics to assist with diagnosis, treatment planning and patient monitoring — but the rules governing how these systems are approved, monitored and held accountable haven't kept pace. The Regulatory Review flags a growing 'governance gap' where AI tools are being deployed in clinical settings without adequate oversight frameworks. This matters to everyday people because it means the AI helping diagnose your condition may not have gone through the same rigorous checks as a new drug or medical device.

sport.summary: NRL Round 23 kicks off tonight with the Titans hosting the Cowboys at Cbus Super Stadium on the Gold Coast. The AFL trade and injury rumour mill is spinning hard, and Filipino tennis star Alex Eala is making waves in Toronto.

stories.title: Titans host Cowboys tonight at Cbus Super Stadium — Indigenous Round derby
stories.why_it_matters: The Titans are backing themselves to get up against the Cowboys tonight in what the club is calling an Indigenous Round derby. Gold Coast fans should expect a fired-up Cowboys outfit — North Queensland are always dangerous — but the Titans are feeling confident at home. Kick-off is 7:50 PM at Cbus Super Stadium, right in your backyard.

stories.title: Souths fans divided after two players granted immediate NRL releases
stories.why_it_matters: South Sydney has granted two players immediate releases to sign with rival NRL clubs — a move that's split the Rabbitohs' fanbase. The club faces Parramatta in Round 23 this Saturday night. Player movements at this point of the season can signal either a rebuild is underway or that there's tension inside the club — either way, it's a distraction heading into a tough match.

stories.title: Warriors lock down early Dally M favourite ahead of Round 23 clash with Panthers
stories.why_it_matters: The Warriors have reportedly locked up an early Dally M Medal (the NRL's player of the year award) favourite on a new contract — a sign of confidence from the Auckland club ahead of their Friday night clash with Penrith. The Panthers are still considered premiership contenders, so this is a big game for the Warriors' top-eight ambitions.

stories.title: AFL team tips: Collingwood star misses training, mass Adelaide changes loom
stories.why_it_matters: Collingwood has a star missing training this week — doubts growing on their availability for this weekend — while Adelaide is set for mass selection changes. The AFL finals race is tightening and every selection call matters. No player names were confirmed in available reporting, but the Pies and Crows both have significant decisions to make heading into the weekend.

stories.title: Alex Eala keeps Toronto run alive with three-set win over Alycia Parks
stories.why_it_matters: Filipino tennis star Alex Eala defeated American Alycia Parks 6-1, 4-6 in a hard-fought three-set match to advance at the WTA 1000 National Bank Open in Toronto — one of the biggest events on the women's tour outside the Grand Slams. Eala continues to be one of Asia's most exciting young tennis players and this result keeps her campaign alive at a prestigious event.
